blocks.x: MATH 157 · Algebra 10

The full calculus toolkit for finding derivatives — from the first-principles limit definition, through the product, quotient and chain rules, to derivatives of logarithmic, exponential and trigonometric functions, implicit and parametric differentiation, and the real-world applications of gradients, rates of change, maxima/minima, kinematics and business economics.

6core differentiation rules — constant, power, chain, product, quotient & generalised power 5applications of differentiation — tangents/normals, rates of change, small changes, maxima/minima, curve sketching 2real-world domains covered — linear kinematics and business/economics
By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Differentiate from first principles using f'(x) = limh→0 [f(x+h) − f(x)] / h, and apply the constant, power, sum/difference, product, quotient and generalised power rules.
2Differentiate logarithmic, exponential and trigonometric functions — natural log, general log base b, e^f(x), a^f(x), sin/cos/tan and their powers — using the chain rule throughout.
3Use implicit differentiation for equations that cannot be solved explicitly for y, find higher-order derivatives, and differentiate parametric representations using dy/dx = (dy/dt)·(dt/dx).
4Find tangents, normals, stationary points and points of inflection, test them with the second derivative, determine intervals of increase/decrease, and sketch curves systematically.
5Apply derivatives to rates of change and small-change approximation, and to real kinematics (velocity, acceleration) and business economics (marginal cost, revenue and profit).

blocks.x: Key definitions

The derivative f'(x) = limh→0 [f(x+h) − f(x)] / h — the limiting value of the gradient of the chord AB as Δx → 0. This process is called differentiating from first principles. It gives the instantaneous rate of change of y with respect to x, and the gradient function of the curve y = f(x).

Differentiability implies continuity If f is differentiable at x = a, then f is continuous at x = a. The converse is false — continuity does not imply differentiability (e.g. f(x) = |x| is continuous but not differentiable at x = 0).

Stationary point A point on a curve where dy/dx = 0 — the tangent is parallel to the x-axis. The second derivative d²y/dx² tests its nature: negative ⇒ maximum, positive ⇒ minimum, zero ⇒ possible inflection.
Marginal function In business, the marginal cost/revenue/profit function is the derivative of the corresponding total function — the approximate change from producing one additional unit.
First Principles & Rules→ Log, Exp & Trig→ Implicit & Higher-Order→ Curve Analysis→ Kinematics & Business
Where derivatives come from

Every rule of differentiation is built on the limit definition of the derivative. This section derives it, then builds up the toolkit: constant, power, sum/difference, product, quotient, chain and generalised power rules.

Gradient of a chord → gradient of a tangent For points A(x, f(x)) and B(x+h, f(x+h)) on y = f(x), the chord AB has slope m = [f(x+h) − f(x)] / h. As h → 0, this approaches the gradient of the tangent at A — the derivative, written dy/dx or f'(x).
Differentiating x² from first principles
Find f'(x) from first principles for f(x) = x².

items: 1Write the limit definition of the derivative.f'(x) = lim_{h→0} [f(x+h) − f(x)] / h
2Substitute f(x+h) = (x+h)² and f(x) = x².= lim_{h→0} [(x+h)² − x²] / h
3Expand (x+h)² = x² + 2xh + h², then cancel x².= lim_{h→0} [2xh + h²] / h
4Factor out h from the numerator and cancel with the denominator h.= lim_{h→0} (2x + h)
5Let h → 0.= 2x

blocks.x: Answer: f'(x) = 2x
Find f'(x) from first principles for f(x) = 1/x².

items: 1Set up the limit and combine the fraction over a common denominator.f'(x) = lim_{h→0} [1/(x+h)² − 1/x²] / h
2Combine into a single fraction.= lim_{h→0} [x² − (x+h)²] / [h·x²(x+h)²]
3Expand the numerator: x² − (x² + 2xh + h²) = −2xh − h².= lim_{h→0} [−h(2x+h)] / [h·x²(x+h)²]
4Cancel h, then let h → 0.= lim_{h→0} −(2x+h) / [x²(x+h)²] = −2x / x⁴

blocks.x: Answer: f'(x) = −2/x³
Rules of Differentiation

c: If f(x) = xⁿ, n any real number, then f'(x) = nx^(n−1)
If y = k·g(x), k constant, then dy/dx = k·g'(x)
If h(x) = f(x) ± g(x), then h'(x) = f'(x) ± g'(x)

blocks.x: Differentiate f(x) = 2x³ + 3.

items: 1Apply the power rule to 2x³ (bring down the exponent, subtract 1).d/dx(2x³) = 3·2x^(3−1) = 6x²
2The derivative of the constant 3 is 0.d/dx(3) = 0

blocks.x: Answer: f'(x) = 6x²
Differentiating a product of two functions
Product rule If h(x) = f(x)·g(x), where f and g are differentiable, then h'(x) = f'(x)g(x) + f(x)g'(x).
Differentiate h(x) = 3x³(x⁴ + 2).

items: 1Identify f(x) = 3x³ and g(x) = x⁴ + 2, then find their derivatives.f'(x) = 9x², g'(x) = 4x³
2Apply h'(x) = f'(x)g(x) + f(x)g'(x).h'(x) = 9x²(x⁴+2) + 3x³(4x³)
3Expand each product.= 9x⁶ + 18x² + 12x⁶
4Collect like terms.= 21x⁶ + 18x²

blocks.x: Answer: h'(x) = 21x⁶ + 18x²
Differentiating a ratio of two functions
Quotient rule If h(x) = f(x)/g(x), g(x) ≠ 0, then h'(x) = [f'(x)g(x) − f(x)g'(x)] / [g(x)]².
Differentiate f(x) = (x+3)/(x−2).

items: 1Identify the top and bottom and their derivatives.f(x)=x+3, f'(x)=1; g(x)=x−2, g'(x)=1
2Apply the quotient rule.h'(x) = [1·(x−2) − (x+3)·1] / (x−2)²
3Simplify the numerator: (x−2) − (x+3) = −5.= −5 / (x−2)²

blocks.x: Answer: h'(x) = −5/(x−2)²
Non-differentiable functions
Show that f(x) = |x| is not differentiable at x = 0.

items: 1Form the difference quotient at 0.f'(0) = lim_{h→0} [|h| − 0]/h = lim_{h→0} |h|/h
2Evaluate the left-hand limit (h→0⁻, so |h|=−h).lim_{h→0⁻} |h|/h = −1
3Evaluate the right-hand limit (h→0⁺, so |h|=h).lim_{h→0⁺} |h|/h = 1
4Since the left and right limits disagree, the two-sided limit does not exist.−1 ≠ 1 ⟹ f'(0) does not exist

blocks.x: f(x) = |x| is not differentiable at x = 0 (it has a "corner" there).

Differentiability always implies continuity, but continuity does not necessarily imply differentiability. A function fails to be differentiable at a point where it has a sharp corner, a vertical tangent, or is discontinuous.
Differentiating composite functions
The Chain Rule For a composite function h(x) = f(g(x)), with y = f(u) and u = g(x): dy/dx = dy/du · du/dx.
Find the derivative of f(x) = (5x³ + 3x)⁴ using the chain rule.

items: 1Let u = 5x³ + 3x (the "inside" function), so y = u⁴.du/dx = 15x² + 3
2Differentiate the outer function with respect to u.dy/du = 4u³
3Multiply dy/du by du/dx and substitute u back.dy/dx = 4(5x³+3x)³ · (15x²+3)

blocks.x: Answer: dy/dx = 4(15x² + 3)(5x³ + 3x)³
y = (ax + b)ⁿ and y = {u(x)}ⁿ

Generalised power rule If u is a differentiable function of x and n is any real number, and f(x) = {u(x)}ⁿ, then f'(x) = n{u(x)}^(n−1)·u'(x). In simple terms, if y = (ax+b)ⁿ, then dy/dx = n(ax+b)^(n−1) · a.
Find dy/dx for y = (2x − 5)^(−4).

items: 1Identify a = 2, b = −5, n = −4. Bring the exponent down and reduce it by 1.dy/dx = −4(2x−5)^(−5) · d/dx(2x−5)
2The derivative of the inner linear function 2x − 5 is 2.dy/dx = −4(2x−5)^(−5) · 2
3Multiply the constants together.= −8(2x−5)^(−5)

blocks.x: Answer: dy/dx = −8/(2x−5)⁵
Find the derivatives of:

items: y = (x² + 2)⁵
y = (3x⁴ − 5)⁷
f(x) = ∛(2x − 4) (using the chain rule with a fractional power)

sections.title: Derivatives of the six trigonometric functions

blocks.x: Special function derivatives

Beyond polynomials: the derivative rules for natural and general logarithms, natural and general exponentials, and the six trigonometric functions — all combined with the chain rule for composite arguments.
Derivative of ln x If f(x) = ln x with x > 0, then f'(x) = 1/x. In general, if y = ln f(x), then dy/dx = f'(x)/f(x).
Compute the derivative of f(x) = ln(x⁴ − 2x).

items: 1Identify the inner function f(x) = x⁴ − 2x and its derivative.d/dx(x⁴ − 2x) = 4x³ − 2
2Apply dy/dx = f'(x)/f(x): derivative of inner over the inner itself.dy/dx = (4x³ − 2)/(x⁴ − 2x)

blocks.x: Answer: dy/dx = (4x³ − 2)/(x⁴ − 2x)
Determine the derivative of y = (ln x)².

items: 1Treat this as u², where u = ln x. Apply the chain rule.dy/dx = 2(ln x)^1 · d/dx(ln x)
2The derivative of ln x is 1/x.dy/dx = 2 ln x · (1/x)

blocks.x: Answer: dy/dx = (2 ln x)/x
General logarithmic function For f(x) = log_b{g(x)}, b > 0, b ≠ 1: convert using change of base f(x) = ln{g(x)}/ln b, giving f'(x) = (1/ln b) · g'(x)/g(x).
Differentiate y = log₅(3x + 9).
Answer: dy/dx = 3 / [(3x+9) ln 5]

Derivative of the exponential function For h(x) = e^f(x): h'(x) = e^f(x) · f'(x). For the general exponential f(x) = a^x (a > 0, a ≠ 1), derived using logarithmic differentiation: dy/dx = aˣ ln a; in general, for y = a^f(x): dy/dx = a^f(x) · f'(x) · ln a.
Differentiate g(x) = e^(6x − ½x⁶) using the exponential rule.

items: 1Identify f(x) = 6x − ½x⁶ and find its derivative.f'(x) = 6 − 3x⁵
2Apply h'(x) = e^f(x) · f'(x).g'(x) = e^(6x−½x⁶) · (6 − 3x⁵)

blocks.x: Answer: g'(x) = (6 − 3x⁵)e^(6x−½x⁶)
Prove dy/dx = aˣ ln a for y = aˣ using logarithmic (implicit) differentiation.

items: 1Take the natural log of both sides of y = aˣ.ln y = x ln a
2Differentiate both sides with respect to x implicitly (ln a is a constant).(1/y)(dy/dx) = ln a
3Multiply both sides by y, then substitute y = aˣ back in.dy/dx = y · ln a = aˣ ln a

blocks.x: Answer: dy/dx = aˣ ln a
Find dy/dx for y = 5^(9x − 5).

items: 1Identify f(x) = 9x − 5, f'(x) = 9, and base a = 5.dy/dx = a^f(x) · f'(x) · ln a
2Substitute all values in.dy/dx = 5^(9x−5) · 9 · ln 5

blocks.x: Answer: dy/dx = 9(ln 5) · 5^(9x−5)
Derivatives of the six trigonometric functions

Chain rule for trig composites
If y = sin f(x), then dy/dx = f'(x) cos f(x). If y = cos f(x), then dy/dx = −f'(x) sin f(x).
Differentiate y = sin(x² − 3x + 1).

items: 1Identify the inner function f(x) = x² − 3x + 1 and its derivative.f'(x) = 2x − 3
2Apply dy/dx = f'(x) cos f(x).dy/dx = (2x−3) cos(x² − 3x + 1)

blocks.x: Answer: dy/dx = (2x − 3) cos(x² − 3x + 1)

Powers of trig functions
If y = cosⁿ x, then dy/dx = n cos^(n−1) x · d/dx(cos x) = −n sin x cos^(n−1) x. Similarly, if y = sinⁿ x, then dy/dx = n sin^(n−1) x cos x.
Differentiate y = tan² x.

items: 1Treat as u², u = tan x, and apply the power rule with the chain rule.dy/dx = 2 tan^1 x · d/dx(tan x)
2The derivative of tan x is sec² x.dy/dx = 2 tan x · sec² x

blocks.x: Answer: dy/dx = 2 tan x sec² x
Differentiate y = x³ cos 2x (product rule combined with the chain rule).

items: 1Identify f(x) = x³ and g(x) = cos 2x, with derivatives.f'(x) = 3x², g'(x) = −2 sin 2x
2Apply the product rule h' = f'g + fg'.dy/dx = 3x² cos 2x + x³(−2 sin 2x)

blocks.x: Answer: dy/dx = 3x² cos 2x − 2x³ sin 2x
Beyond y = f(x)

Not every curve is given as y = f(x). This section covers differentiating equations that mix x and y, repeating differentiation to get second/third derivatives, and handling curves defined via a parameter t.

Implicit function
A function in two variables x and y where neither can be expressed explicitly in terms of the other, e.g. x² + y² = 3xy. To differentiate implicitly: (1) differentiate term by term to get an equation in dy/dx, x and y; (2) make dy/dx the subject.

Key implicit-differentiation facts d/dx(y) = dy/dx; d/dx(y²) = 2y·dy/dx; d/dx(2y³) = 6y²·dy/dx; in general d/dx(f(y)) = f'(y)·dy/dx. Terms like 3x²y, xy, x·dy/dx are treated as products; terms like x²/y are treated as quotients.
Circle equation
Use implicit differentiation to find dy/dx for x² + y² = 25.

items: 1Differentiate each term with respect to x. d/dx(x²) = 2x; d/dx(y²) = 2y·dy/dx (chain rule, since y is a function of x); d/dx(25) = 0.2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0
2Isolate the dy/dx term.2y(dy/dx) = −2x
3Divide both sides by 2y.dy/dx = −2x/2y

blocks.x: Answer: dy/dx = −x/y
Use implicit differentiation to find dy/dx for 3xy + 6y² = 15.

items: 1Differentiate 3xy using the product rule: d/dx(3xy) = 3y + 3x(dy/dx). Differentiate 6y² using the chain rule: d/dx(6y²) = 12y(dy/dx).3y + 3x(dy/dx) + 12y(dy/dx) = 0
2Group the dy/dx terms on one side, other terms on the other.(3x + 12y)(dy/dx) = −3y
3Divide both sides by (3x + 12y) and simplify.dy/dx = −3y / (3x+12y) = −y/(x+4y)

blocks.x: Answer: dy/dx = −y / (x + 4y)
Second and third derivatives
Notation Differentiating dy/dx again gives the second derivative d²y/dx² = f''(x); differentiating once more gives the third derivative d³y/dx³ = f'''(x), and so on.
Find dy/dx, d²y/dx² and d³y/dx³ for y = x⁴ − x³ + 4x − 1.

items: 1Differentiate term by term using the power rule.dy/dx = 4x³ − 3x² + 4
2Differentiate dy/dx again.d²y/dx² = 12x² − 6x
3Differentiate d²y/dx² once more.d³y/dx³ = 24x − 6

blocks.x: dy/dx = 4x³−3x²+4, d²y/dx² = 12x²−6x, d³y/dx³ = 24x−6
Curves defined by x = f(t), y = g(t)
Parametric derivative For x = f(t) and y = g(t) with parameter t: dy/dx = (dy/dt) · (dt/dx), where dt/dx = 1 / (dx/dt) (since we can only directly find dx/dt, not dt/dx).
If x = t² and y = t³, find dy/dx in terms of t and confirm the curve is y = x^(3/2).

items: 1Differentiate x and y with respect to t.dx/dt = 2t, dy/dt = 3t²
2Apply dy/dx = (dy/dt) ÷ (dx/dt).dy/dx = 3t² / 2t = (3/2)t
3To confirm the Cartesian form: eliminate t using t = √x (from x=t²), so y = t³ = (√x)³ = x^(3/2).y = x^(3/2) ⟹ dy/dx = (3/2)x^(1/2) = (3/2)√x = (3/2)t ✓

blocks.x: Answer: dy/dx = 3t/2, consistent with y = x^(3/2)
Use implicit differentiation to determine dy/dx for:

items: y³ − 4x² − 7 = 0
4e^y = x²
x²y² − 7x³ − 5 = 0

blocks.x: And find dy/dx in terms of t for x = at², y = 2at (a constant).

sections.title: Equations of the tangent and normal

blocks.x: Geometry from derivatives

The gradient function unlocks the full geometric behaviour of a curve: its tangent and normal lines, how quantities change together, how to approximate small changes, where it turns, and how to sketch it accurately.

The gradient function If y = f(x), then dy/dx or f'(x) is the gradient function. The gradient of the curve at point P(a,b) is dy/dx evaluated at (a,b), written dy/dx|₍ₐ,ᵦ₎ — the same as the gradient of the tangent to the curve at P.
Equations of the tangent and normal

Tangent and normal formulas If m = dy/dx|₍ₐ,ᵦ₎ is the gradient of the tangent at P(a,b), then the tangent is y − b = m(x − a). The normal is perpendicular to the tangent at P; if m₁ is the tangent's gradient and m₂ the normal's, then m₁ · m₂ = −1.
Find the equations of the tangent and normal to y = x³ − 3x + 2 at P(2, 4).

items: 1Differentiate to get the gradient function.dy/dx = 3x² − 3
2Evaluate the gradient at x = 2 to get m₁.m₁ = 3(2)² − 3 = 12 − 3 = 9
3Write the tangent equation using y − b = m(x − a) with (a,b) = (2,4).y − 4 = 9(x − 2) ⟹ y = 9x − 14
4Find the normal's gradient from m₁·m₂ = −1.m₂ = −1/9
5Write the normal equation through the same point (2,4).y − 4 = −(1/9)(x − 2) ⟹ 9y = −x + 38

blocks.x: Tangent: y = 9x − 14. Normal: 9y = −x + 38
Related quantities changing together

Rate of change If y depends on and varies with x, the rate of change of y with respect to x is dy/dx. If y is increasing with x, dy/dx > 0; if decreasing, dy/dx < 0. Rates of change are, by convention, with respect to time.
A spherical balloon is inflated so its volume increases at 2 cm³/s. Find the rate of increase of the radius when V = 50 cm³. [V = (4/3)πr³]

items: 1Differentiate V with respect to r.dV/dr = 4πr²
3Use the chain rule dr/dt = (dr/dV)·(dV/dt), where dr/dV = 1/(dV/dr).dr/dt = (1/4πr²) × 2
4Substitute r ≈ 2.285 and evaluate.dr/dt = 2/(4π(2.285)²) ≈ 0.0305

blocks.x: Answer: dr/dt ≈ 0.03 cm/s
Approximating Δy using dy/dx
Small-change approximation Since Δy/Δx ≈ dy/dx for small Δx, Δy ≈ (dy/dx) · Δx. For a percentage change of p% in x: Δx = (p/100)x, and the approximate percentage change in y is (Δy/y) × 100.
If y = √x, find the approximate increase in y as x increases from 4 to 4.01.

items: 1Differentiate y = x^(1/2).dy/dx = (1/2)x^(−1/2) = 1/(2√x)
2Evaluate dy/dx at x = 4, and identify Δx = 4.01 − 4 = 0.01.dy/dx|_{x=4} = 1/(2·2) = 1/4

blocks.x: Answer: Δy ≈ 0.0025
Finding and classifying stationary points

Procedure for testing stationary points (a) Find dy/dx and d²y/dx². (b) Put dy/dx = 0 and solve for the turning value(s) of x. (c) Substitute back into y = f(x) to get the y-coordinate. (d) Substitute x into d²y/dx²: if < 0, it's a maximum; if > 0, it's a minimum; if = 0, it may be an inflection point.
Find the stationary points of f(x) = x³ − 6x² − 15x − 1 and determine their nature.

items: 1Differentiate to get the gradient function, and differentiate again for the second derivative.f'(x) = 3x² − 12x − 15, f''(x) = 6x − 12
2Set f'(x) = 0 and solve. Divide by 3, then factor.x² − 4x − 5 = 0 ⟹ (x−5)(x+1) = 0 ⟹ x = 5 or x = −1
3Find the y-coordinates by substituting into f(x).f(5) = 125−150−75−1 = −101; f(−1) = −1−6+15−1 = 7
4Classify using f''(x): at x=5, f''(5)=30−12=18>0 (minimum); at x=−1, f''(−1)=−6−12=−18<0 (maximum).x=5: min; x=−1: max

blocks.x: Maximum at (−1, 7); minimum at (5, −101)
A rectangular sheet of metal 60cm by 50cm has squares of side x cm cut from each corner and the sides folded up to form an open box of volume V. Find x for maximum volume.

items: 1The base becomes (60−2x) by (50−2x), height x, so V(x) = x(60−2x)(50−2x).V = 4x³ − 220x² + 3000x
2Differentiate and set dV/dx = 0.dV/dx = 12x² − 440x + 3000 = 0
3Divide by 4: 3x² − 110x + 750 = 0. Solve with the quadratic formula.x = [110 ± √(110² − 4·3·750)] / (2·3) = [110 ± √3100]/6
4√3100 ≈ 55.68, giving x ≈ 27.6 or x ≈ 9.05. Since 2x must be less than 50, reject x ≈ 27.6.x ≈ 9.05 cm

blocks.x: Answer: x ≈ 9.05 cm gives the maximum volume
Sign of the derivative
Increasing / decreasing test If dy/dx > 0 on an interval, the function is increasing there. If dy/dx < 0, it is decreasing.
Find the range of x for which f(x) = x³ − 12x + 5 is increasing.

items: 1Differentiate.f'(x) = 3x² − 12
2Set f'(x) > 0 and solve the inequality: 3x² > 12, so x² > 4.x² − 4 > 0 ⟹ (x−2)(x+2) > 0
3This product is positive when both factors agree in sign: x < −2 or x > 2.x < −2 or x > 2

blocks.x: Answer: f is increasing for x < −2 or x > 2
A 3-step systematic procedure

Step 1 — Intercepts
For the x-intercept, put y = 0 and solve for x. For the y-intercept, put x = 0 and solve for y.

Step 2 — Turning points
Put dy/dx = 0 and solve for x, then substitute into y = f(x) for the y-coordinate(s).

Step 3 — Classify with d²y/dx²
d²y/dx² > 0 ⟹ minimum; d²y/dx² < 0 ⟹ maximum; d²y/dx² = 0 ⟹ inflection point.
Prepare to sketch y = x(x² − 16) — find its intercepts and turning points.

items: 1x-intercepts: set y = 0. x(x²−16)=0 ⟹ x(x−4)(x+4)=0.x = 0, 4, −4
2y-intercept: set x = 0.y = 0
3Expand y = x³ − 16x, differentiate, and set to 0.dy/dx = 3x² − 16 = 0 ⟹ x = ±√(16/3) ≈ ±2.31
4Classify with d²y/dx² = 6x: positive at x≈2.31 (min), negative at x≈−2.31 (max).x≈2.31: min; x≈−2.31: max

blocks.x: x-intercepts: −4, 0, 4. Turning points near x ≈ ±2.31 (max at −2.31, min at 2.31)
Real-world applications
Two major domains where differentiation drives real decisions: the motion of a particle (displacement, velocity, acceleration) and the economics of production (marginal cost, revenue and profit).

Displacement, velocity & acceleration For a particle with displacement x = f(t): velocity v = dx/dt is the rate of change of displacement; acceleration a = dv/dt is the rate of change of velocity. If v = 0, the particle is momentarily at rest; if v < 0, it moves opposite to its initial direction; if a > 0 it accelerates, if a < 0 it decelerates.
Average velocity & acceleration Average velocity = (x₂ − x₁)/(t₂ − t₁) = Δx/Δt. Average acceleration = (v₂ − v₁)/(t₂ − t₁) = Δv/Δt.
Particle in straight-line motion

A particle moves so that its distance x metres from a fixed point after t seconds is x(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t. Find (a) the times at which it is stationary, (b) its distance at those times, (c) its acceleration at those times.

items: 1The particle is stationary when velocity v = dx/dt = 0.v = 3t² − 12t + 9
2Set v = 0, divide by 3, and factor.t² − 4t + 3 = 0 ⟹ (t−1)(t−3) = 0 ⟹ t = 1, 3
3Substitute t=1 and t=3 into x(t) for the distances.x(1)=1−6+9=4; x(3)=27−54+27=0
4Differentiate v to get acceleration a = dv/dt = 6t − 12, then evaluate at t=1 and t=3.a(1) = 6−12 = −6; a(3) = 18−12 = 6

blocks.x: Stationary at t=1 (x=4, a=−6 m/s², decelerating) and t=3 (x=0, a=6 m/s², accelerating)
A ball is thrown vertically upward with height h(t) = 32t − 8t² metres after t seconds. Find (a) its velocity at t=1, (b) the maximum height reached.

items: 1Differentiate h(t) to get velocity.v(t) = dh/dt = 32 − 16t
2Substitute t = 1 to find the velocity there.v(1) = 32 − 16 = 16 m/s
3Maximum height occurs when v = 0: 32 − 16t = 0 ⟹ t = 2.t = 2 s
4Substitute t = 2 into h(t) for the maximum height.h(2) = 32(2) − 8(4) = 64 − 32 = 32

blocks.x: Velocity at t=1: 16 m/s. Maximum height: 32 m (at t=2s)
Cost, revenue, profit — and their marginals

c: R(x) = x·P(x), where P(x) is price-demand

blocks.x: Marginal analysis The marginal of any function is the approximate change in that quantity from producing one additional unit — precisely, the derivative of the corresponding total function.
Condition for maximum profit π'(x) = R'(x) − C'(x); for maximum profit π'(x) = 0, so R'(x) = C'(x) — marginal revenue equals marginal cost. Also π''(x) < 0 (from R''(x) < C''(x)) confirms a maximum.

Condition for minimum average cost Since AC(x) = C(x)/x, differentiating with the quotient rule and setting d/dx(AC) = 0 gives C'(x) = C(x)/x — average cost is minimised when marginal cost equals average cost.
Marginal cost & average cost
A company's cost of producing x items is C(x) = 2680 + 2x + 0.001x². Find the marginal cost function, and the marginal cost at x = 300.

items: 1The marginal cost function is the derivative of C(x).MC(x) = C'(x) = 2 + 0.002x

blocks.x: Answer: MC(300) = 2.6 (approx. cost of the 301st item)
Cost and price-demand functions are C(x) = 680 + 4x + 0.01x², P(x) = 12. Find the production level that maximises profit.

items: 1Form the revenue function R(x) = xP(x), then the profit function π(x)=R(x)−C(x).R(x) = 12x; π(x) = 12x − (680+4x+0.01x²) = −0.01x² + 8x − 680
2For maximum profit, set MR(x) = MC(x), i.e. π'(x) = 0.π'(x) = −0.02x + 8 = 0
3Solve for x.0.02x = 8 ⟹ x = 400
4Confirm it's a maximum: π''(x) = −0.02 < 0. ✓π''(x) = −0.02 < 0 (maximum confirmed)

blocks.x: Answer: profit is maximised at a production level of x = 400 units
